newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia Sept retail trade.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia Sept retail trade.

text.p: Australian retail sales fell 3.7 percent in September and rose 0.6 percent in the September quarter, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
Economists' forecasts had centred on a monthly fall of 0.5 percent and a 1.3 percent quarterly rise. A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follows:
SHANE OLIVER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, AMP INVESTMENTS:

"This confirms the analysis coming from elsewhere that the Australian economy is currently relatively soft. Combined with low inflation and signs that wages growth is slowing, this definitely points to the Reserve Bank easing. I think there'll now be a bit more debate about the magnitude of that easing."
ROB HENDERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER INTERNATIONAL:

"These numbers are very weak obviously. There was room for a correction after the strong July and August figures but in my view these numbers are weaker than a statistical correction so the underlying consumption level in the economy looks very weak. I think the chance of a rate cut next week is now better than a 50-50 chance. When you combine this number with the skilled vacancy survey, poor exports in the balance of payments data, the building approvals numbers, and the CPI numbers it is all pointing now to a very weak economy and I can't see a lot can be gained now by holding off for another month."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"The data is reinforcing some of the pessimistic views that are coming from the corporate sector. The retailers have been screaming for several months how things are pretty tough. I think the rate cut next week looks highly probable. I suspect there's a few worries here for the policy makers, and the economy may be weaker than they were thinking just a month when the RBA Bulletin came out."
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MACQUARIE BANK:

"There's no doubt that this weaker-than-expected result has added to the case for a rate cut. And that's even after allowing for the early fall of Fathers' Day, which saw department store sales rise very strongly in August and unwinding in September. There's still a good chance for the Reserve Bank to ease next week. But they're going to want to see some moderation in the Department of Industrial Relations' wage settlements data before they cut rates."
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"It is a big shock obviously. You don't usually see falls as big as this. It is clearly overstated but nevertheless it does mean we are not going to get as much contribution from retail trade in the September quarter as we thought and so we are looking at a weaker growth story. But the retail sector has not fallen in this much of a hole but the strength from the previous two months was also overstated. Any decision about (a rate cut) next week has already been made, but with what we got yesterday (building approvals) this basically suggests that this economy is in need of a rate cut. We assume we will get one next week."
CRAIG JAMES, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"The Reserve Bank has little reason to delay a rate cut now based on today's data. The only sticking point that they have got to delay a rate cut is concern about entreprise bargaining agreements. The economic evidence, survey evidence and anecdotal evidence is overwhelming that the economy now needs a monetary stimulus."
